contentBlocks.text: Let's count! Look around your room — how many windows do you see? How many chairs? Today we'll practice counting real things, one at a time, all the way up to 20.

Gather 20 small objects — blocks, buttons, coins, or dried beans all work. Line them up in a row. Touch each object once as you say its number out loud: 1, 2, 3... Move slowly. If you lose count, start over from 1 — that's normal and okay! Once you can count to 10 without help, try counting all the way to 20.

objectives: Count a set of up to 20 objects, saying one number name for each object (one-to-one correspondence)
Recognize that the last number said tells how many objects are in the set (cardinality)
materialsNeeded: 20 small objects per child (blocks, buttons, coins, or dried beans)
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Sit with the child and place a small pile of objects between you.
2. Model counting 5 objects first: move each one to a new pile as you say its number aloud, touching each object exactly once.
3. Ask the child to try the same with 5 objects, then 10.
4. Watch for two common mistakes: skipping an object (undercounting) and touching one object while saying two numbers (overcounting). Gently pause and recount together when this happens — don't rush to correct, let them try again.
5. Once 10 is comfortable, extend to counting all 20 objects.
6. Finish with the worksheet: the child counts each group of pictures and writes the matching number.
differentiationTips: Struggling: stay at counting to 10 for now; use bigger, more spaced-out objects so touching one-at-a-time is easier
Ready for more: after counting 20 objects, ask 'what if we had one more? What number comes next?'
For a child who already writes numerals confidently, have them write the count themselves instead of circling it
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Counting to 20 with one-to-one correspondence and cardinality is foundational Kindergarten number sense — the base every later Math course (place value, addition, subtraction) builds on.
